text:
alex: Heads up — after yesterday's kernel selection change we’re seeing lower prefix cache hit-rates for a couple prompt cohorts and a couple transient GPU OOMs. Not sure if this is pure eviction/TTL behavior or an interaction with new batching heuristics.

simon: Ugh. Which cohorts? numbers?

alex: Quick snapshot from sampling: pre-change hit-rate ~78%, post-change ~51% for onboarding_flow cohort. Another small cohort (email-summary) fell 20 pts. These are prefixes that share long common prefixes but different suffixes.

maya: That feels like key bonding frag issue — if kernel change altered KV layout or how we normalize keys we could be getting worse collision/entropy -> more unique keys in GPU cache -> fragmentation. Any profiling traces?

alex: Pasted a short capture:
```
perf profile --cohort=onboarding_flow --window=30s --out=onboard.pf
batcher: dynamic -> max_batch 16 (used to cap at 8)
kernel selected: scaled_attention_v2 (fallback path previously scaled_attention_v1 for short seqs)
KV ops: put_rate +24% , evict_rate +18%
GPU mem free curve shows small free islands then OOM on pod-3
LOG: OOM when allocating 512MB arena at 0x7f9c...
```

cheng: Interesting — increasing max_batch and different kernel could increase live KV cache pressure (longer lifetimes for KV entries in GPU). Also scaled_attention_v2 changes KV layout (different per-head packing) which might increase per-key footprint.

ryan: Can we confirm whether per-key size changed? Maybe quantized kernel uses different ephemeral buffers.

maya: Ran a micro-run: same prefix set, compare kernel footprints:
```
per-key-gpu-bytes (v1): median 1.2KB, p95 3.4KB
per-key-gpu-bytes (v2): median 1.6KB, p95 4.8KB
cache occupancy +33% with v2 for same keys
```

alex: That explains it. More bytes per cached key -> earlier evictions + fragmentation -> small cohorts lose hit-rate. Also our eviction is pure global LRU with 1s TTL; not great for cohorts with many similar prefixes.

cheng: Proposal: 1) short-term rollback of kernel selection for small-seq cohorts while we fix kernel packing. 2) tune eviction to segmented LRU: keep a tiny sticky segment for high-frequency prefixes (cohort bloom), 3) increase CPU-side cache budget for hot prefix replicas to reduce GPU fill.

ryan: Also consider warmup priming: on rollout we should prime KV with sampled keys for affected cohorts. A lightweight prefill job that writes the top N prefixes into GPU cache over a minute to avoid bursty warms.

maya: I sketched an experiment config:
```json
{
  "cohorts": ["onboarding_flow","email-summary"],
  "eviction": {"policy":"segmented_lru","segments":[{"name":"sticky","size_pct":10,"ttl_s":120},{"name":"main","size_pct":90,"ttl_s":1}]},
  "prefill": {"enabled":true,"top_n":5000,"ramp_ms":60000},
  "kernel_override": {"scaled_attention_v2":"disable_for"}
}
```
(put as experiment id: cache-bonding-1967)

alex: Nice. For observability, add per-cohort cache-key-entropy metric + per-key-size histogram. We need to detect perf regressions early in rollout.

infra-bot: deploy-plan created: experiment/cache-bonding-1967 -> canary 5% -> monitor: hit-rate-cohort, evict-rate, gpu-ooms, p95-latency.

cheng: One more note on fragmentation mitigation: we can try a compact-on-free sweep when fragmentation crosses threshold (coalesce slabs). That is slightly disruptive but avoids cascade OOMs. Schedule as a fallback after 10% OOM spike.

ryan: Agree. Also add a conservative kernel selection rule: avoid switching to kernels that increase per-key footprint by >15% for rollout <=10% traffic. We'll run local microbench for packing delta.

alex: Action items:
- maya: run the experiment and collect 24h traces (cohort-specific)
- cheng: implement segmented_lru prototype + slab coalesce hook (P0 for on-call safety)
- ryan: add kernel footprint check to compile-time selection stats
- simon: coordinate a rollback path for the last kernel rollout if canary shows regressions

simon: I’ll own rollback path and smoke test.

alex: Thanks — let’s sync in 2h. If you hit OOMs, abort canary and run slab-coalesce immediately. :thumbsup:
